claim: Maintaining stable body temperature through environmental thermal stressors requires detection of temperature changes, relay of information, and coordination of physiological and behavioral responses.
source: Maintaining stable body temperature through environmental thermal stressors requires detection of temperature changes, relay of information, and coordination of physiological and behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a general statement about thermoregulation that draws from established scientific understanding of homeostatic processes.

claim: Studies have implicated areas in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) as nodes in the thermosensory neural circuitry.
source: Studies have implicated areas in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) as nodes in the thermosensory neural circuitry and indicate that the opioid system within the POA is vital in regulating body temperature.
evidence: This claim references prior studies without specific citations in this sentence, indicating it draws from established literature.

claim: The opioid system within the POA is vital in regulating body temperature.
source: Studies have implicated areas in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) as nodes in the thermosensory neural circuitry and indicate that the opioid system within the POA is vital in regulating body temperature.
evidence: This claim references prior studies indicating the importance of the opioid system in thermoregulation.

claim: Neurons projecting to the POA from PBN express the opioid peptides dynorphin and enkephalin.
source: In the present study we identify neurons projecting to the POA from PBN expressing the opioid peptides dynorphin and enkephalin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Warm-activated PBN neuronal populations overlap with both prodynorphin (Pdyn) and proenkephalin (Penk) expressing PBN populations.
source: Using mouse models, we determine that warm-activated PBN neuronal populations overlap with both prodynorphin (Pdyn) and proenkephalin (Penk) expressing PBN populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from warm exposure and immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: In the PBN, Prodynorphin (Pdyn) and Proenkephalin (Penk) mRNA expressing neurons are partially overlapping subsets of a glutamatergic population expressing Solute carrier family 17 (Slc17a6) (VGLUT2).
source: Here we report that in the PBN Prodynorphin (Pdyn) and Proenkephalin (Penk) mRNA expressing neurons are partially overlapping subsets of a glutamatergic population expressing Solute carrier family 17 (Slc17a6) (VGLUT2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FISH data showing co-expression patterns.

claim: Pdyn, Penk, and VGLUT2 expressing PBN neurons are critical for physiological and behavioral heat defense.
source: Our findings demonstrate that Pdyn, Penk, and VGLUT2 expressing PBN neurons are critical for physiological and behavioral heat defense.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by optogenetic and chemogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Maintaining body temperature in the face of changing environmental conditions is a core attribute of mammals, including humans, and is critical for life.
source: Maintaining body temperature in the face of changing environmental conditions is a core attribute of mammals, including humans, and is critical for life.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about mammalian physiology.

claim: Achieving a stable body temperature requires information about the temperature of the periphery and environment to be integrated to drive physiological and behavioral programs to defend the core temperature.
source: Achieving a stable body temperature requires information about the temperature of the periphery and environment to be integrated to drive physiological and behavioral programs to defend the core temperature (Jessen, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jessen, 1985.

claim: Physiological parameters modulated to maintain temperature include thermogenesis (utilization of brown adipose tissue [BAT], shivering), changes in circulation (vasodilation and vasoconstriction), and evaporation.
source: Physiological parameters modulated to maintain temperature include thermogenesis (utilization of brown adipose tissue [BAT], shivering), changes in circulation (vasodilation and vasoconstriction), and evaporation (Cabanac, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cabanac, 1975.

claim: Behavioral modifications include selection, when possible, of ambient temperature, altering posture to alter heat loss, and modulation of physical activity level.
source: Behavioral modifications include selection, when possible, of ambient temperature, altering posture to alter heat loss, and modulation of physical activity level.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of thermoregulatory behaviors.

claim: Responding to thermal challenges involves perception of temperature, encoding the valence of the temperature (e.g. too hot), and evoking appropriate physiological responses.
source: Responding to thermal challenges involves perception of temperature, encoding the valence of the temperature (e.g. too hot), and evoking appropriate physiological responses (Tan and Knight, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tan and Knight, 2018.

claim: Perceptive, affective, and autoregulatory elements may be encoded by overlapping or discrete neuronal circuits.
source: Perceptive, affective, and autoregulatory elements may be encoded by overlapping or discrete neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential neural organization.

claim: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) have been identified as key nodes within the neurocircuitry regulating body temperature.
source: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) have been identified as key nodes within the neurocircuitry regulating body temperature.
evidence: This is a statement based on established literature in the field.

claim: The POA contains neurons critical for integration of information about body temperature and for coordination of responses to thermal challenges to maintain core temperature.
source: The POA contains neurons critical for integration of information about body temperature and for coordination of responses to thermal challenges to maintain core temperature (Abbott and Saper, 2017; Abbott and Saper, 2018; Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abbott and Saper, 2017; Abbott and Saper, 2018; Tan et al., 2016.

claim: Neurons in POA, identified by different genetic markers, can regulate BAT activation, drive vasodilation, and shift ambient temperature preferences.
source: Neurons in POA, identified by different genetic markers, can regulate BAT activation, drive vasodilation, and shift ambient temperature preferences (Tan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tan et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2016.

claim: Prior evidence has suggested critical roles for inputs from the PBN to the POA in regulating temperature.
source: Prior evidence has suggested critical roles for inputs from the PBN to the POA in regulating temperature (Geerling et al., 2016; Miyaoka et al., 1998; Morrison, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Geerling et al., 2016; Miyaoka et al., 1998; Morrison, 2016.

claim: The PBN is a highly heterogenous structure with subpopulations known to relay various sensory information from the periphery (thirst, salt-appetite, taste, pain, itch, temperature, etc.).
source: The PBN is, however, a highly heterogenous structure with subpopulations known to relay various sensory information from the periphery (thirst, salt-appetite, taste, pain, itch, temperature, etc.) and playing key roles in nocifensive responses, specifically escape and aversive learning (Chiang et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Palmiter, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Palmiter, 2018.

claim: The PBN plays key roles in nocifensive responses, specifically escape and aversive learning.
source: The PBN is, however, a highly heterogenous structure with subpopulations known to relay various sensory information from the periphery (thirst, salt-appetite, taste, pain, itch, temperature, etc.) and playing key roles in nocifensive responses, specifically escape and aversive learning (Chiang et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Palmiter, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiang et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Palmiter, 2018.

claim: Regulation of body temperature requires integration of homeostatic and environmental inputs across varying time scales creating opportunities for neuromodulatory signaling to play key roles.
source: Regulation of body temperature requires integration of homeostatic and environmental inputs across varying time scales creating opportunities for neuromodulatory signaling to play key roles.
evidence: This is an inference about the role of neuromodulation in thermoregulation based on the complexity of the process.

claim: In vivo experiments suggest that opioid neuropeptides, as a neuromodulator, may play a critical role in thermal homeostasis.
source: In vivo experiments suggest that opioid neuropeptides, as a neuromodulator, may play a critical role in thermal homeostasis.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior experimental evidence in the literature.

claim: Pharmacologic manipulation of opioid systems induces changes in body temperature and can impair thermoregulatory control in humans, rats, and other animals.
source: Pharmacologic manipulation of opioid systems induces changes in body temperature and can impair thermoregulatory control in humans, rats, and other animals (Chen et al., 2005; Ikeda et al., 1997; Spencer et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005; Ikeda et al., 1997; Spencer et al., 1990.

claim: Opioid receptor signaling within the POA has been implicated in modulating body temperature, but potential sources for native ligands remain to be identified.
source: Opioid receptor signaling within the POA has been implicated in modulating body temperature, but potential sources for native ligands remain to be identified (Baker and Meert, 2002; Clark, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baker and Meert, 2002; Clark, 1979.

claim: Activation of mu receptors in the POA can drive opposing effects on body temperature.
source: Activation of mu receptors in the POA can drive opposing effects on body temperature.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior research on opioid receptor function.

claim: Neurons in PBN expressing prodynophin (Pdyn), which is processed to dynorphin, the endogenous ligand for the kappa opiate receptor (KOR), are activated by ambient warmth.
source: A recent study indicated that neurons in PBN expressing prodynophin (Pdyn), which is processed to dynorphin, the endogenous ligand for the kappa opiate receptor (KOR), are activated by ambient warmth (Chavkin et al., 1982; Geerling et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chavkin et al., 1982; Geerling et al., 2016.

claim: PBN neurons expressing the endogenous mu and delta opioid receptor ligand, enkephalin, have not been examined in relation to how they may regulate temperature.
source: PBN neurons expressing the endogenous mu and delta opioid receptor ligand, enkephalin, have not been examined in relation to how they may regulate temperature.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Exposure to ambient warmth (38°C) for 4 hr induces Fos expression in the lateral PBN (LPBN).
source: Consistent with recent reports, we observed induction of Fos expression in the lateral PBN (LPBN) (Figure 1B,C; Geerling et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry and is consistent with prior reports (Geerling et al., 2016).

claim: In brain sections from warm exposed mice (n = 8) compared to room temperature controls (n = 4), there was a significant (p=0.003) increase in mean ± SEM number of neurons positive for Fos expression in the LPBN per brain: 265.8 ± 41.9 in warm exposed mice compared to 23.2 ± 4.0 in room temperature controls.
source: In brain sections from warm exposed mice (n = 8) compared to room temperature controls (n = 4), Fos staining revealed a robust and significant (p=0.003) increase in mean ± SEM number of neurons positive for Fos expression in the LPBN per brain: 265.8 ± 41.9 in warm exposed mice compared to 23.2 ± 4.0 in room temperature controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In brains from recombinase reporter mice (Ai14) crossed to Pdyn-Cre (Ai14xPdyn-Cre) or Penk-Cre (Ai14xPenk-Cre) lines, tdTomato was robustly expressed in LPBN indicating expression of Pdyn and Penk in LPBN neurons.
source: In brains from recombinase reporter mice (Ai14) crossed to Pdyn-Cre (Ai14xPdyn-Cre) or Penk-Cre (Ai14xPenk-Cre) lines, tdTomato was robustly expressed in LPBN indicating expression of Pdyn (Al-Hasani et al., 2015; François et al., 2017; Krashes et al., 2014; Madisen et al., 2010) and Penk (François et al., 2017) in LPBN neurons (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using Cre-reporter mice and is consistent with prior characterization of these lines.

claim: Cells expressing tdTomato in Pdyn-Cre mice (Pdyn+) and Penk-Cre mice (Penk+) were most abundant in the caudal LPBN.
source: Cells expressing tdTomato in Pdyn-Cre mice (Pdyn+) and Penk-Cre mice (Penk+) were most abundant in the caudal LPBN.
evidence: This is an observation from anatomical analysis of reporter expression.

claim: In the LPBN of Ai14xPdyn-Cre mice, a mean ± SEM of 81% ± 2.5 of the cells positive for Fos staining were also positive for tdTomato expression (n = 4 animals, 1017 cells).
source: In the LPBN of Ai14xPdyn-Cre mice, we found that a mean ± SEM of 81% ± 2.5 of the cells positive for Fos staining were also positive for tdTomato expression (n = 4 animals, 1017 cells) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data analyzing co-expression.

claim: In the LPBN of Ai14xPenk-Cre mice, an average ± SEM of 54% ± 4.6 (n = 4 animals, 1109 cells) of Fos-positive cells in warm-exposed mice were also positive for tdTomato.
source: In the LPBN of Ai14xPenk-Cre mice, an average ± SEM of 54% ± 4.6 (n = 4 animals, 1109 cells) of Fos-positive cells in warm-exposed mice were also positive for tdTomato (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data analyzing co-expression.

claim: In samples from Ai14xPdyn-Cre mice, 22% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells) of tdTomato neurons in the LPBN were also labeled for Fos.
source: We blindly sampled tdTomato neurons in the LPBN and then quantified the number of cells also labeled for Fos. In samples from Ai14xPdyn-Cre mice we found 22% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells) overlap and from Ai14xPenk-Cre 18% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data analyzing co-expression in the reverse direction.

claim: In samples from Ai14xPenk-Cre mice, 18% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells) of tdTomato neurons in the LPBN were also labeled for Fos.
source: We blindly sampled tdTomato neurons in the LPBN and then quantified the number of cells also labeled for Fos. In samples from Ai14xPdyn-Cre mice we found 22% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells) overlap and from Ai14xPenk-Cre 18% ± 4 (n = 3 animals, 150 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data analyzing co-expression in the reverse direction.

claim: Warmth activated neurons in LPBN may co-express the neuropeptides dynorphin and enkephalin.
source: These data indicate that warmth activated neurons in LPBN may co-express the neuropeptides dynorphin and enkephalin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap data showing that both Pdyn+ and Penk+ cells are activated by warmth.

claim: A mean ± SEM of 98% ± 0.9 (n = 760 cells, n = 4 mice) of Pdyn labeled cells were positive for Slc17a6.
source: A mean ± SEM of 98% ± 0.9 (n = 760 cells, n = 4 mice) of Pdyn labeled cells were positive for Slc17a6 (Figure 2A,I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments showing co-expression.

claim: A mean ± SEM of 97% (n = 650 cells, n = 4 mice) of Penk labeled cells were positive for Slc17a6.
source: A mean ± SEM of 97% (n = 650 cells, n = 4 mice) of Penk labeled cells were positive for Slc17a6 (Figure 2B,J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments showing co-expression.

claim: A mean ± SEM of 51% ± 6.6 (n = 760, n = 4 mice) of LPBN neurons positive for Pdyn were also positive for Penk labeling.
source: Surprisingly, a mean ± SEM of 51% ± 6.6 (n = 760, n = 4 mice) of LPBN neurons positive for Pdyn were also positive for Penk labeling (Figure 2C,K).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments showing co-expression.

claim: A mean ± SEM of 58% ± 2.3 (n = 650 cells, n = 4 mice) of cells labeled by Penk probes were also labeled by Pdyn probes.
source: Reciprocally, a mean ± SEM of 58% ± 2.3 (n = 650 cells, n = 4 mice) of cells labeled by Penk probes were also labeled by Pdyn probes (Figure 2D,K).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments showing co-expression.

claim: Pdyn+ and Penk+ cells in the LPBN express Slc17a6 and are partially overlapping subpopulations of glutamatergic LPBN cells.
source: These FISH based experiments indicate that Pdyn+ and Penk+ cells in the LPBN express Slc17a6 and are partially overlapping subpopulations of glutamatergic LPBN cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH data showing co-expression patterns.

claim: 70% ± 0.7 (mean ± SEM, n = 150 cells, n = 3 mice) of LBP Pdyn labeled neurons were co-labeled by Cck probes.
source: We examined if Pdyn labeled neurons in LPBN were co-labeled by probes for Cck and found that 70% ± 0.7 (mean ± SEM, n = 150 cells, n = 3 mice) of LBP Pdyn labeled neurons were co-labeled by Cck probes (Supplemental Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F) suggesting that mRNA for Cck and pDyn is expressed in overlapping neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments showing co-expression.

claim: mRNA for Cck and pDyn is expressed in overlapping neuronal populations.
source: We examined if Pdyn labeled neurons in LPBN were co-labeled by probes for Cck and found that 70% ± 0.7 (mean ± SEM, n = 150 cells, n = 3 mice) of LBP Pdyn labeled neurons were co-labeled by Cck probes (Supplemental Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–F) suggesting that mRNA for Cck and pDyn is expressed in overlapping neuronal populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-labeling data.

claim: VGLUT2+, Pdyn+, and Penk+ neurons from the PBN project to POA including the VMPO.
source: VGLUT2+, Pdyn+, and Penk+ neurons from the PBN project to POA including the VMPO (Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing experiments using anterograde and retrograde viral approaches.

claim: Pdyn+PBN→POA neurons represent a subset of the VGLUT2+PBN→POA population.
source: Pdyn+PBN→POA neurons represent a subset of the VGLUT2+PBN→POA population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viral tracing and FISH data showing that Pdyn+ cells express VGLUT2.

claim: All of the projecting PBN neurons to POA are VGLUT2+.
source: Results obtained with retro-AAV Cre-switch, red (tdTomato) to green (GFP), injections into the POA revealed that all of the projecting PBN neurons are VGLUT2+ and a subset are Pdyn+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by viral tracing experiments showing only GFP+ cells in VGLUT2-Cre mice.

claim: Of GFP labeled cells in the LPBN, 49 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) were labeled by both Penk and Pdyn probes (n = 3 mice, 169 cells).
source: We found that of GFP labeled cells in the LPBN, 49 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) were labeled by both Penk and Pdyn probes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments on retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: 13 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of GFP labeled LPBN neurons were not labeled by either Pdyn or Penk probes (n = 3 mice, 169 cells).
source: 13 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of the quantified GFP labeled LPBN neurons were not labeled by either Pdyn or Penk probes (n = 3 mice, 169 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from FISH experiments on retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: Photostimulation of PdynPBN→POA neuron terminals caused rapid and significant reduction in body temperature in Pdyn-Cre mice (n = 6).
source: Photostimulation of PdynPBN→POA neuron terminals caused rapid and significant reduction in body temperature in Pdyn-Cre mice (n = 6), with increasing magnitude of drop in body temperature corresponding to increasing photostimulation frequency up to 10 Hz (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments with quantitative measurements.

claim: 15 min of stimulation of PdynPBN→POA projections reduced the body temperature to 36.0 ± 0.1°C at 2 Hz (p=0.571 vs. control), 33.3 ± 0.6°C (p=0.0032) at 5 Hz, 31.9 ± 0.3°C, (p<0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 31.9 ± 0.4°C (p<0.0001) at 15 Hz compared to control.
source: 15 min of stimulation of PdynPBN→POA projections reduced the body temperature to 36.0 ± 0.1°C at 2 Hz (p=0.571 vs. control), 33.3 ± 0.6°C (p=0.0032) at 5 Hz, 31.9 ± 0.3°C, (p<0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 31.9 ± 0.4°C (p<0.0001) at 15 Hz compared to control.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from optogenetic experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: In control mice (n = 7), photostimulation did not cause significant changes in body temperature at any of the tested frequencies.
source: In control mice (n = 7), photostimulation did not cause significant changes in body temperature at any of the tested frequencies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a control finding from optogenetic experiments.

claim: Photostimulation of PenkPBN→POA neuron terminals caused a rapid reduction in body temperature in a stimulation frequency dependent manner.
source: Photostimulation of PenkPBN→POA neuron terminals also caused a rapid reduction in body temperature (Figure 4E) in a stimulation frequency dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments.

claim: 15 min of stimulation of PenkPBN→POA projections in Penk-Cre mice reduced body temperature to 36.4 ± 0.3°C at 2 Hz (p=0.999 vs. control), 34.9 ± 0.7°C (p=0.495) at 5 Hz, 33.8 ± 0.3°C (p=0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 33.7 ± 0.4°C (p=0.0002) at 15 Hz.
source: 15 min of stimulation of PenkPBN→POA projections in Penk-Cre mice reduced body temperature to 36.4 ± 0.3°C at 2 Hz (p=0.999 vs. control), 34.9 ± 0.7°C (p=0.495) at 5 Hz, 33.8 ± 0.3°C (p=0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 33.7 ± 0.4°C (p=0.0002) at 15 Hz, compared to a separate cohort of control mice (n = 7) which did not display altered body temperatures in response to photostimulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from optogenetic experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: In VGLUT2-Cre mice with AAV-DIO-ChR2-eYFP injected into PBN, stimulation of VGLUT2PBN→POA terminals in POA caused a rapid and significant decrease in body temperature.
source: In VGLUT2-Cre mice with AAV-DIO-ChR2-eYFP injected into PBN, stimulation of VGLUT2PBN→POA terminals in POA also caused a rapid and significant decrease in body temperature (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from optogenetic experiments.

claim: 15 min of photostimulation in VGLUT2-Cre mice (n = 8) significantly reduced the mean ± SEM body temperature to 36.5 ± 0.5°C at 2 Hz (p=0.257 vs. control) 34.0 ± 0.5°C at 5 Hz (p=0.0005), 32.8 ± 0.3°C (p<0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 32.9 ± 0.2°C (p<0.0001) at 15 Hz compared to control mice (n = 7).
source: 15 min of photostimulation in VGLUT2-Cre mice (n = 8) significantly reduced the mean ± SEM body temperature to 36.5 ± 0.5°C at 2 Hz (p=0.257 vs. control) 34.0 ± 0.5°C at 5 Hz (p=0.0005), 32.8 ± 0.3°C (p<0.0001) at 10 Hz, and 32.9 ± 0.2°C (p<0.0001) at 15 Hz compared to control mice (n = 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from optogenetic experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The average changes in body temperature measured in Pdyn-Cre and VGLUT2-Cre mice were not significantly different at any of the tested stimulation frequencies.
source: The average changes in body temperature that we measured in Pdyn-Cre and VGLUT2-Cre mice were not significantly different at any of the tested stimulation frequencies.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The body temperature reduction evoked by photostimulation in Penk-Cre mice was smaller in magnitude than that in either Pdyn-Cre or VGLUT-Cre mice.
source: The body temperature reduction evoked by photostimulation in Penk-Cre mice was smaller in magnitude than that in either Pdyn-Cre or VGLUT-Cre mice.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The mean body temperature measured in Penk-Cre mice after 15 min of simulation was significantly different than Pdyn-Cre at 10 Hz (p=0.02), with activation of the Penk+ terminals having less of an effect.
source: The mean body temperature we measured in Penk-Cre mice after 15 min of simulation was significantly different than Pdyn-Cre at 10 Hz (p=0.02), with activation of the Penk+ terminals having less of an effect.
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Activation of PBN→POA terminals causes rapid decreases in body temperature.
source: These data demonstrate that activation of PBN→POA terminals causes rapid decreases in body temperature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In Pdyn-Cre mice, mean ± SEM eye temperature dropped from 36.9°C ± 0.3 to 32.8°C ± 0.2 with 15 min of stimulation.
source: In Pdyn-Cre mice, mean ± SEM eye temperature dropped from 36.9°C ± 0.3 to 32.8°C ± 0.2 with 15 min of stimulation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from thermal imaging experiments.

claim: In Pdyn-Cre mice, tail temperature measurements demonstrated a very rapid increase following the onset of photostimulation, increasing a mean ± SEM of 4.2°C ± 0.5 after 2 min of photostimulation.
source: In Pdyn-Cre mice, tail temperature measurements demonstrated a very rapid increase following the onset of photostimulation, increasing a mean ± SEM of 4.2°C ± 0.5 after 2 min of photostimulation (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from thermal imaging experiments.

claim: Increase in tail temperature preceded the decline in core body temperature.
source: Increase in tail temperature preceded the decline in core body temperature.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal dynamics of the thermal imaging data.

claim: At baseline, there was a mean ± SEM difference of 6.9 ± 0.29°C between the measured eye and tail temperatures.
source: At baseline we observed a mean ± SEM difference 6.9 ± 0.29°C between the measured eye and tail temperatures.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from thermal imaging experiments.

claim: Eye–tail temperature difference significantly (p<0.0001) decreased compared to control to a mean ± SEM of 1.3 ± 0.3°C and remained stable during photostimulation even as body temperature declined.
source: Eye–tail temperature difference significantly (p<0.0001) decreased compared to control to a mean ± SEM of 1.3 ± 0.3°C and remained stable during photostimulation even as body temperature declined.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from thermal imaging experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The difference in eye–tail temperature returned to baseline shortly after photostimulation was stopped.
source: The difference in eye–tail temperature returned to baseline shortly after photostimulation was stopped (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an observation from thermal imaging experiments showing reversibility.

claim: In Pdyn-Cre mice, the temperature of the BAT region decreased rapidly following the onset of stimulation and returned to baseline post-stimulation in a pattern similar to body temperature.
source: In Pdyn-Cre mice, the temperature of the BAT region decreased rapidly following the onset of stimulation and returned to baseline post-stimulation in a pattern similar to body temperature (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is an observation from thermal imaging experiments.

claim: The temperature difference between BAT and eye (BAT–eye) decreased during the period of stimulation but returned to baseline when stimulation was stopped.
source: The temperature difference between BAT and eye (BAT–eye) decreased during the period of stimulation but returned to baseline when stimulation was stopped (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is an observation from thermal imaging experiments.

claim: In the Penk-Cre mice, photostimulation of PenkPBN→POA terminals led to a decrease in eye temperature, a rapid increase in tail temperature, decrease in BAT temperature, and collapse of the eye–tail temperature gradient.
source: In the Penk-Cre mice, we found similar effects, but of smaller overall amplitude. Photostimulation of PenkPBN→POA terminals led to a decrease in eye temperature, a rapid increase in tail temperature, decrease in BAT temperature, and collapse of the eye–tail temperature gradient (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is an observation from thermal imaging experiments in Penk-Cre mice.

claim: PBN to POA neurons can drive physiologic adaptation to lower body temperature by increasing heat dissipation and suppressing thermogenesis.
source: Together these results indicate that PBN to POA neurons can drive physiologic adaptation to lower body temperature by increasing heat dissipation and suppressing thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the thermal imaging and body temperature data.

claim: 30 min after treatment with naltrexone, there was no significant impact on photostimulation induced change in body temperature compared to saline treated animals in Pdyn-Cre mice.
source: 30 min after treatment with naltrexone, we did not observe a significant impact on photostimulation induced change in body temperature compared to saline treated animals.
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments testing the role of opioid receptors.

claim: Pretreatment with norBNI did not significantly alter the decrease in body temperature induced by 10 Hz photostimulation of PdynPBN→POA terminals.
source: Pretreatment with norBNI did not significantly alter the decrease in body temperature induced by 10 Hz photostimulation of PdynPBN→POA terminals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments testing the role of kappa opioid receptors.

claim: Pretreatment with naltrexone or norBNI mitigated U50 mediated suppression of locomotor activity.
source: Pretreatment with naltrexone or norBNI mitigated U50 mediated suppression of locomotor activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating the effectiveness of the antagonist treatments.

claim: 30 min after treatment with naloxone, no significant effect on photostimulation-induced changes in body temperature was observed in Penk-Cre mice.
source: 30 min after treatment with naloxone, PenkPBN→POA terminals were photostimulated at 10 Hz. No significant effect of naloxone on photostimulation-induced changes in body temperature was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments testing the role of opioid receptors.

claim: The acute alterations in body temperature due to stimulation of PdynPBN→POA and PenkPBN→POA terminals are not driven by endogenous opioid release and subsequent opioid receptor signaling.
source: These data suggest that the acute alterations in body temperature due to stimulation of PdynPBN→POA and PenkPBN→POA terminals are not driven by endogenous opioid release and subsequent opioid receptor signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments with opioid antagonists.

claim: Glutamatergic signaling in the POA and in PBN has previously been implicated in heat defensive behaviors.
